productionMl.name: Active Learning — Labeling Pipeline
productionMl.description: Labeling large volumes of sensor data is the bottleneck in every production ML cycle, and the labels that already exist are not necessarily right. I led development of labeling workflows built around Active Learning, so the pipeline ranks which samples are worth a human's attention instead of working the queue in order — and runs the same scoring pass over already-annotated data, where disagreement between model and label surfaces likely mislabels.
productionMl.imageAlt: Active-learning loop: a model trains on the labeled data pool, identifies uncertain samples in the unlabeled pool, and requests human review, which feeds new labels back into training.

productionMl.name: Performance Analysis — Overfit Mapping
productionMl.description: Models that look strong in the lab do not always hold up at inference time, and an aggregate accuracy number hides where they fail. I built analytical tooling that compares lab and production behaviour and maps where a model overfits and underfits across its input space, turning a single metric into a picture of which regions are actually trustworthy — wired into the release path so the check runs before deployment, not after.
highlights: Gates every release · ~3 bugs caught per model
productionMl.imageAlt: Lab versus production model behaviour side by side: clean converging accuracy curves in the lab, degraded and unstable curves in deployment, with a heatmap magnified to locate the failing regions.

productionMl.name: Time-Series Anomaly Detection & Enrichment
productionMl.role: Data Science Analyst @ DRS RADA Technologies
productionMl.description: Sensor time-series arrives noisy, and the noise costs twice — once in training time, once in detection accuracy. I developed time-series analysis, forecasting and anomaly-detection algorithms with signal-noise and outlier reduction ahead of training, and separately automated data enrichment and labeling by integrating external APIs with tracking systems to recover signal the pipeline had been dropping.
highlights: Forecasting + anomaly detection on sensor streams
Noise and outlier reduction ahead of training
In production · thousands of tracks recovered
productionMl.imageAlt: The two costs of unrefined sensor data: a noisy time-series stream lengthening the training cycle, and anomalies hidden inside that noise reducing detection accuracy.

independent.name: Northbeam Support Copilot
independent.description: A tool-calling support agent for a fictional radar company, built so a support engineer can ask in plain language and get an answer that shows its work. Twelve read-only tools in three layers — records, calculation, retrieval — run in a bounded loop; their real results become the evidence for one structured call. The interesting decision is the refusal layer: where the right answer is enumerable, deterministic rules decide the outcome rather than the model, so 62% of declines are settled in code and the card can say which rule fired.
highlights: 12 read-only tools across records, calculation and hybrid BM25 + embedding policy search
Deterministic refusal layer — 62% of declines decided in code, not by the model
196 offline tests · 77 graded evals · trace-based KPI dashboard
independent.imageAlt: The copilot's operational KPI dashboard: latency and token counts per call, tool-usage bars, and a breakdown of which outcomes were decided in code rather than by the model.

independent.name: Beat the ASPP
independent.description: Multi-agent equity research that decomposes the problem the way a research desk does. Three specialist agents — technical, fundamental, sentiment — run in parallel, each with its own tools and Pydantic-enforced output, then a strategist agent reconciles them into one verdict. The decision worth stealing is two-stage write-then-extract: Opus writes the narrative, Sonnet extracts the JSON, which holds the quality and costs roughly five times less than asking one model for both.
highlights: Three analyst agents in parallel; a strategist reconciles one defensible verdict
Opus writes the prose, Sonnet extracts the JSON — same quality, ~5× cheaper
Provider abstraction across Anthropic / Groq / Ollama, with per-call cost telemetry
independent.imageAlt: The app in use: a holdings table and allocation breakdowns, a per-position trade chart, and the analyst panel running a scan across a watchlist of tickers.

independent.name: Menu Alchemist
independent.description: Photograph a drink or a menu and get the reconstructed recipe — ingredients, steps, glassware, estimated ABV — plus a shopping list of only what you don't already own. The split is the point: the vision model does extraction and nothing else, while pantry detection, package sizing, serving maths and retailer matching are pure Python, so the part that has to be right every time is unit-tested rather than prompted.
highlights: Pluggable vision providers behind one interface — Gemini, local Ollama, or a fake for tests
Vision model extracts; deterministic Python decides what actually reaches the buy list
86 tests that need no network and no API key · installable PWA · deployed on Render
independent.imageAlt: Menu Alchemist demo: a photographed cocktail menu becomes a reconstructed recipe and a buy list of only the bottles you don't own.
